author: Halvard Ulfsson, Archivist of the Northern Courts
pages:
#Foreword

Every child of the north can recite the names of the old kings, but few can tell you what those kings actually did. This little book is meant for travellers, merchants and curious youths who would like to know how the cold country came to be ruled the way it is, without wading through forty volumes of court records.

I have kept to what the chronicles agree upon. Where they quarrel, I say so.

#The First Landing

The first Nords did not arrive as conquerors. They came across the northern sea in long open boats, fleeing a homeland the chroniclers call only the Old Shore. The songs say five hundred ships set out and fewer than two hundred saw land.

They found a country of black rock, pine and snow, already home to elves who had little love for strangers. The settlers built their first halls from overturned hulls, and for a generation they did little more than survive the winters.

It was the hunting and the hard ground, the old saying goes, that made the Nords what they are: stubborn, loud at the table and quiet in the field.

#The Hall of Many Chieftains

For three centuries there was no single crown. Each valley had its chieftain, and each chieftain had a mead hall, a temper and a grudge against at least two neighbours. Feuds over grazing land could last longer than the families who began them.

What finally bound the clans together was not love but fear. When the elves of the eastern forests marched west, the chieftains understood that a hundred small halls would burn one by one. They met at a frozen lake, cut a ring into the ice, and swore to follow whoever could hold the ring longest against all challengers.

The winner was a shield-maiden named Brynja Coldhand. She ruled for thirty-one years, and every king since has been crowned standing on a ring of stone in her memory.

#The Years of Iron and Salt

Under Brynja's heirs the Nords pushed south and east. Their armies crossed mountain passes that the elves had thought impassable, and for a time the Nordic Empire stretched far beyond the snows. Southern lords sent tribute in salt, wine and silver, and the halls of the north grew rich.

But an empire built on raids must keep raiding. When the plunder slowed, the jarls began to quarrel over what remained. The southern provinces slipped away one by one, some by rebellion, some simply because no one bothered to collect their taxes.

#The War of the Two Crowns

The empire's last great disaster was a succession dispute. When old King Sigvald died without naming an heir, both his daughter and his nephew claimed the stone ring. The holds split down the middle. Brothers who had shared a bench at the same table met across a frozen river and killed each other.

The war lasted nine years and settled nothing. In the end both claimants were dead, and the jarls agreed to choose future kings by council rather than by birth. This custom, called the Moot, survives to this day, though it is honoured more in speeches than in practice.

#What Remains

The Nordic Empire is gone, but its bones are everywhere. The old roads follow the routes its armies marched. The barrows on the hillsides hold its warriors, and, if the stories are true, not all of them rest easily.

When you see a ring of stones on a hilltop, or a burial mound with a door sealed in bronze, remember that someone once believed this country would be ruled from that place forever. Empires are proud things. Winters are patient ones.
